name: Fergburger
label: Fergburger
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/336415647: the OpenStreetMap point 'Fergburger'.
notes: Famous burger shop with queues on Shotover Street.

text.description: Fergburger is a burger restaurant on Shotover Street in the middle of Queenstown. It began in February 2001 in a garage off Cow Lane, where it was hard to find and grew mainly through word of mouth. It now sits on Shotover Street beside its bakery, Ferg Baker, which opened in 2011, and a bar that opened in July 2020. The menu is built around gourmet burgers, including lamb, venison, cod, falafel and tofu versions. For a photo, the appeal is the street scene rather than a grand view: the shopfront, the signs and the people gathering outside give a feel for everyday Queenstown. A simple wide shot of the frontage with the street leading towards it tells the story well. Keep the shop name in the frame and leave a little space around it so the shot does not look cramped. If you want a close-up of a burger or the bakery counter, ask politely and keep out of the way of other customers.
text.geographic_location: Fergburger is on Shotover Street in central Queenstown, next to its own bakery, Ferg Baker, and its bar.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops serve this spot, so start from the centre of Queenstown and head for Shotover Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the shopfront. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow or you want the whole street. Use telephoto (2x or more) for details such as the signage.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front entrance, 42 Shotover Street). The shop front with the queue forming outside, framed by the street. Stay on the pavement and out of the doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the shopfront up on one of the vertical lines so it looks straight. Include some of the street in the foreground. Take a second, tighter shot with the telephoto of the sign or the people outside.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the shopfront to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is washing out. In the evening, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against a post or wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter for a clean shot of the street, while dusk gives glowing signs and shopfronts.

text.access_note: Fergburger is a working restaurant on a public street, so you can photograph it from the pavement, but check the official site before you go for anything about visiting inside.

name: Queenstown Gardens
label: Queenstown Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Queenstown Gardens' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Queenstown Gardens' (way/30473059): edge nearest the subject (977 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/30473059: large area 'Queenstown Gardens' (980 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Peninsula park with lake and mountain views.

text.description: Queenstown Gardens fills the peninsula beside the town centre, with Lake Wakatipu on several sides. It is a botanical garden with a large pond, tall Douglas firs and a mix of native and exotic trees. The first two oaks were planted in 1866 and the gardens opened officially in 1867. For photographs, the best place is the tip of the peninsula, which looks south across the lake. From there the water fills the foreground and The Remarkables ridge rises on the far side. Late afternoon is the time to aim for, when the peaks pick up golden light. The gardens have other good subjects too. The rose garden dates from the 1960s, when 850 bushes were planted, and the Scott Memorial from 1913 is also worth a look. Trails run through the trees with views of the mountains, the Frankton Arm and the town. For a close-up scene rather than a lake panorama, try the arched bridge framed by trees and reflected in the pond, which looks best in autumn colour. For a wider view, the gardens and lake can also be seen from One Mile Carpark above the town, with The Remarkables and Walter Peak behind. Sunny summer days are busy, so go early if you want the paths to yourself.
text.geographic_location: Queenstown Gardens sits on a peninsula right next to the town centre of Queenstown, with Lake Wakatipu and the Frankton Arm on its sides. The band rotunda stands near the Park Street entrance.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Queenstown and head for the gardens on the lakeside peninsula, which is next to the town. From there, look south-east towards the subject about 100 m away. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Begin with the default lens (1x) for the lake and ridge together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more foreground water or the pond and bridge. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the peaks of The Remarkables.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Queenstown Gardens (tip of the peninsula, facing south across the lake). Lake Wakatipu in the foreground with The Remarkables ridge across the water, best framed in late afternoon light.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower third, depending on whether the water or the mountains are the main subject. Keep a little shoreline in the bottom of the frame for depth. For a different shot, move to the pond and frame the arched bridge between the autumn trees with its reflection below. The view of the gardens and lake from One Mile Carpark is another option.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the peaks to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the golden light is not washed out. Use panorama mode only if you can pan slowly and keep the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or sunset, when the peaks catch golden light. Early morning is quieter, especially on sunny summer days.

text.access_note: Queenstown Gardens is an open public park; check the official site before you go in case of events or seasonal changes, such as the winter LUMA festival.

name: Eichardt's Hotel
label: Eichardt's Hotel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Queenstown Gardens' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Queenstown Gardens' (way/30473059): edge nearest the subject (977 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/246150622: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Eichardt's Private Hotel' (56 m across).
notes: Historic lakefront hotel on Marine Parade.

text.description: Eichardt's Hotel stands on the corner of Marine Parade and Ballarat Street, right on the Lake Wakatipu shore, and is a significant local landmark in Queenstown. The site goes back to the early gold-rush years. William Rees, one of the first European settlers here, had a woolshed on this spot, and after gold turned up in the Shotover River in 1862 he converted it into a hotel called the Queen's Arms. Albert Eichardt joined him in 1866, became sole proprietor by 1869, and his name stuck. The building is listed as a Category Two historic place. It was badly affected by the November 1999 floods, then restored and reopened as Eichardt's Private Hotel in December 2001. It photographs well because it is a solid, characterful building set against open water and mountains, with the rest of the town around it. One suggested viewpoint is the lakefront about 195 m east of the hotel, towards Queenstown Gardens, looking back towards the town. From there you can show the hotel frontage with the lake edge in front of it. A closer, street-level alternative is Marine Parade itself, which gives a straight-on view of the building with the lake and mountains behind. Take a moment to check that trees or passing traffic are not blocking the front of the building, and step a few paces along the shore if they are.
text.geographic_location: Eichardt's Hotel is in central Queenstown, on the lakefront at the corner of Marine Parade and Ballarat Street. The Queenstown Gardens peninsula lies a short walk to the east.
text.directions_text: The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the hotel frontage with the lake edge and town around it. If the building looks too small, switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick it out. Keep the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the wider lake-and-mountain scene, where the hotel will be a small part of the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Queenstown Gardens (lakeshore path on the peninsula, looking back toward the town centre). The hotel's lakefront frontage on Marine Parade, seen across the lake edge from the gardens, with the town around it. From here the hotel's lakefront frontage on Marine Parade sits among the buildings of the town, with the water in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the hotel on one of the vertical lines so the building stands upright rather than leaning. Use the lake edge as a foreground line leading towards it. If you want a closer, straight-on shot, walk to Marine Parade, where the hotel fills more of the frame with the lake and mountains behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the hotel to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky or water is washing out. If you are there at dusk, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, more even light than midday, and the lakeshore tends to be quieter early on.

text.access_note: The hotel is a private, paid-stay property, so the outside can be photographed from public spaces such as the lakefront and Marine Parade, but check the official site before you go if you want to go inside or into the courtyard.
claims_not_in_sources: Queenstown Gardens is a public park on a peninsula east of the town centre, and is the nearby inferred viewpoint area.
Trees on Marine Parade or passing traffic may partly block the view of the hotel frontage.
Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer than midday light.
The lakeshore is usually quieter early in the day.

name: TSS Earnslaw
label: TSS Earnslaw
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Steamer Wharf' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Steamer Wharf' (way/1289605199): middle (74 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OSM N496797308 (TSS Earnslaw): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic coal-fired steamship at the Steamer Wharf.

text.description: Steamer Wharf is Queenstown's historic lakefront pier, and it is the home berth of the TSS Earnslaw, the steamer you will see tied up here. It photographs well because the ship, the water and the Remarkables all sit in one frame. The wharf is also lined with cafés and bars, so it is easy to stop, wait for a good moment and take your time over the shot. If you can, check the ship's departure times beforehand. It sails to a schedule, so the best pictures are of it tied up at the wharf, or of it coming around Queenstown Bay to dock. Start with a simple wide view: the ship on the left or right third of the picture, the lake in front and the mountains rising behind. Then move in for a tighter shot of the funnel and hull, with the water behind. A gallery shot of the ship docked at sunrise above the Remarkables shows how well the setting works at the start of the day. Take a few frames in case people walk through. If you have time for a second angle, Fern Hill is a single example that shows a winter sunset over the lake and the Remarkables, with the Earnslaw on the water. Its exact standing point is unverified, so treat it as an extra rather than a replacement.
text.geographic_location: On the Queenstown Bay lakefront in central Queenstown, on the shore of Lake Wakatipu. The wharf is a pier with cafés and bars around it.
text.directions_text: From the middle of Queenstown, head down to the Queenstown Bay lakefront and look for Steamer Wharf. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the ship with the Remarkables behind it. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the wharf and sky, and telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a close shot of the ship or to make the mountains look bigger behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Steamer Wharf. The steamer tied up at the lakefront wharf in Queenstown Bay, with the Remarkables rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the ship on one of the side lines, with the mountains along the top third. Keep your phone level so the water line stays straight. If you want a different view, Fern Hill is a second example, showing a winter sunset over the lake and the Remarkables with the ship on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the ship to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is washing out. Try a Live Photo as the ship docks, and take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise suits the ship docked below the Remarkables. Whatever time you go, check the ship's departure times first so you know when it will be at the wharf.

text.access_note: The ship sails on a schedule, so check its departure times before you go.

name: Queenstown Hill
label: Queenstown Hill
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Moonlight Track' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Moonlight Track' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3235799661: the OpenStreetMap point 'Queenstown Hill'.
notes: Hill walk with wide views over town and the lake.

text.description:
Queenstown Hill is a small mountain near Queenstown, 907 metres high. It also has a Māori name, Te Tapu-nui, meaning 'mountain of intense sacredness'. Most photos you will see are taken from the hill. This one is of the hill itself, which is the point of this spot. Seen from a distance, it shows the layers of the slope clearly. Houses sit on the lower levels, a band of mainly wilding conifers, including Douglas fir and larch, covers the middle, and the top is open tussock. The hill is also a working sheep farm. That mix of town, forest and bare ridge gives you a layered landscape shot rather than a single dramatic peak.

The view here is from the Moonlight Track above Arthurs Point, on the Shotover River side. The track runs around the flanks of the hill, so you see the hill from the side rather than from the top. Choose a clear gap in the trees and let the ridge fill the upper half of the frame. Keep a little foreground, such as the track edge or a bush, in the lower part to add depth. Stop walking before you take the shot and check the screen for tree branches creeping into the corners.
text.geographic_location: Queenstown Hill is a small mountain near Queenstown, with housing on its lower slopes near Frankton Road and Marina Heights. The viewpoint is on the Moonlight Track above Arthurs Point, on the Shotover River side.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Arthurs Point (check local transport options yourself). From there, join the Moonlight Track on the Shotover River side. Walk until you find a clear gap in the trees where the hill is in view. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone), or the default lens (1x) if you want more of the valley around the hill. The ultra-wide (0.5x) will make the hill look small and distant, so save it for close foreground scenes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Moonlight Track (Shotover River side, from the track above Arthurs Point; the exact standing spot is not identified in the sources). Queenstown Hill seen from the Moonlight Track, the one photo of the hill from a lower, off-summit position that I found. The hill is to the south-east. The exact spot is not fixed along the track, so look for a gap in the trees with an open view of the whole ridge and the bare top.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the ridge line on the upper third. Keep the forest band and the houses below it to show the three layers of the hill. A bit of track or bush in the foreground adds depth. Keep the phone level so the slope doesn't look tilted.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the hill to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the tussock and trees keep their colour. If you zoom to 3x or more, hold the phone with both hands and brace your elbows against your body to keep it sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when lower sun gives the slopes shape and the colours are warmer. Midday light tends to flatten the hillside.

text.access_note: Check access and conditions on the ground or with the official track information before you go, as they can change.
claims_not_in_sources: From the Moonlight Track above Arthurs Point, the hill appears to the south-east of the viewer.
Lower sun in the early morning or late afternoon gives hillsides more shape and warmer colour than midday sun.
Gaps in the trees along the track may give a clear view of the hill, but the best gap varies.

name: Ben Lomond (Otago)
label: Ben Lomond
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ben Lomond Saddle' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/496009090: the OpenStreetMap point 'Ben Lomond'.
notes: Prominent peak above town with a famous summit track.

text.description: Ben Lomond is the big mountain that rises behind Queenstown, reaching 1,748 metres. It was named after Ben Lomond in Scotland by an early shepherd, Duncan McAusland. For a phone photographer, the most rewarding place on it is the Ben Lomond Saddle, a point on the track between the lower slopes and the summit. The saddle is a recommended photo stop on the track below the summit. From the saddle the summit climb rises directly ahead of you. When you turn around, Lake Wakatipu and Queenstown spread out below. The saddle is closer to the peak than the town lookouts, so it works well as a photo stop if you don't plan to go on to the top. The track climbs through Douglas fir forest, then mountain beech, then opens into tussock grassland, so you get changing scenery on the way up. The full summit hike is a 5 to 8 hour return trip of about 11 to 14 km with a lot of climbing, and it is often icy in winter, so many visitors stop at the saddle. The saddle is a point on the track rather than a signed lookout, so check the trail before you go. If you would rather photograph the mountain from a distance, Queenstown Hill gives a wide panorama over the town and lake with Ben Lomond among the surrounding peaks, though there it sits in the background rather than filling the frame.
text.geographic_location: Ben Lomond rises north-west of Queenstown town centre, with its summit about 4 km away. Its lower slopes, including Bob's Peak where the Skyline complex stands, look straight down on the town.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or stops nearby, so head north-west from Queenstown town centre towards the mountain. The track can be joined at the One Mile Carpark, the access road on Lomond Crescent, or the Skyline building on Brecon Street. From any of these, follow the marked track up the ridge to the saddle between Ben Lomond and Bowen Peak. Check current track conditions before you set off. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole slope and sky, and the default lens (1x) for the lake and town behind you. A telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) helps to pick out the summit ridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The suggested photo spot is Ben Lomond Saddle, on the track between the lower slopes and the summit, below the summit itself. Facing uphill, the summit climb rises directly ahead of you. Turn around and Lake Wakatipu and Queenstown are visible below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the track in the lower third of the frame so it leads the eye up to the summit. Then turn round and take a second shot with the lake and town beyond the tussock. If you also visit Queenstown Hill, you can photograph Ben Lomond from there as part of the wider panorama.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the brightest part of the view and lower the exposure slider a little, so the lake and clouds keep their detail. Panorama mode works well for the sweep of the basin if you turn slowly. Keep a firm footing on the track while you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Pick a clear day, and check track conditions first, since the upper track is often icy in winter.

text.access_note: This is a hiking track on open mountain, and the steep route to the summit crosses private land, so check the official site and current track conditions before you go; the Skyline Gondola is a ticketed option for the lower part, so check the official site before you go.

name: Edith Cavell Bridge
label: Edith Cavell Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Edith Cavell Bridge' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Edith Cavell Bridge' (way/917325046): middle (39 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/917325046: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Edith Cavell Bridge' (39 m across).
notes: Historic bridge over the Shotover River at Arthurs Point.

text.description:
Edith Cavell Bridge carries a single-lane road over the Shotover River at Arthurs Point, between Queenstown and Arrowtown. It stands 47.8 metres tall and is a concrete-and-steel arch built between 1917 and 1919. It replaced an older wooden trestle bridge from 1875. Heritage New Zealand lists it as a Category I heritage structure. The name comes from an old gold miner, Jack Clark, who named it in honour of the nurse Edith Cavell and painted the name on a sign and on the bridge itself, even though the council wanted to call it Cooper's Crossing.

It photographs well because of where it sits. From the footpath on the bridge deck you look straight down a narrow canyon, with the gorge walls closing in around the Shotover far below. If the jet boats are running, one may sweep through the frame and give the picture a sense of scale. Walkers can use the footpath while the road stays single-lane, but traffic still passes close by, so stay on the footpath and keep clear of the road while you take your shots.

For something different, the bridge itself is worth a photo from further away. A short walk along Oxenbridge Tunnel Road gives a view of the arch and the canyon together, rather than a view from the deck. The gorge is often in shadow, so go in daylight and expect the light to change as you wait. Check road status before you set off.
text.geographic_location: Edith Cavell Bridge is at Arthurs Point, on the road between Queenstown and Arrowtown, next to the Shotover Jet attraction on the Shotover River.
text.directions_text: The bridge is at Arthurs Point, between Queenstown and Arrowtown, next to the Shotover Jet area. Use the map to get there. Parking nearby is limited, so allow a little extra time. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) on the bridge deck to take in the canyon walls and the river together. Use the default lens (1x) for a tighter view straight down the gorge. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), save it for picking out a jet boat on the water or for the arch from the second viewpoint.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Edith Cavell Bridge (footpath on the bridge deck, looking down the gorge). The Shotover River far below in its narrow canyon, with the gorge walls framing the water, and the jet boats passing through if they are running.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the river on one of the lines so the canyon walls lead the eye into the picture. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. Wait for a jet boat to enter the frame if they are running. As an alternative, walk to Oxenbridge Tunnel Road for a view of the bridge arch and the canyon from a little way off.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the water to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky does not wash out the picture. Try a Live Photo if a boat is passing, so you can pick the best moment afterwards. Hold the phone firmly with both hands, as it is a long way down.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, because the gorge is often in shadow and the light only reaches the canyon at certain hours. Check the picture on your screen and wait for the sun to reach the water if you can.

text.access_note: This is a public road bridge with a footpath, but it is single-lane and has been closed briefly before, so check road status and the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Traffic passes close to the footpath on the bridge deck, so take care when taking photographs.
Parking near the bridge is limited.
A short walk along Oxenbridge Tunnel Road gives a view of the arch and the canyon (the street name comes from a single review, so confirm it on the map).
The light on the water changes through the day, so waiting for the sun to reach the canyon may improve the photo.

name: Skyline Queenstown Gondola
label: Skyline Gondola
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q135683682: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Gondola to the Bob's Peak deck with the classic view over town and Lake Wakatipu.

text.description:
The Skyline Queenstown Gondola climbs Bob's Peak, part of Ben Lomond, to a viewing complex above the town. The top terminal sits about 450 metres above Lake Wakatipu, so the photos here are wide, layered views: rooftops, the lake, and mountain ridges behind. From the viewpoint you can pick out Coronet Peak, The Remarkables, Walter Peak and Cecil Peak, which gives you plenty of different pictures from one spot.

The gondola opened officially on 17 November 1967. The hill was already a popular vantage point, but the steep ground made it hard to reach until a road was cut in 1961. The attraction has been rebuilt in recent years. New gondolas were installed in 2023, a new base terminal and ticketing hall opened in late 2023, and work on the top of Bob's Peak was still going on at the time of writing. Some areas may therefore look different from older photos, or have building work in view.

For phone photos, start with the wide view, then zoom in on one feature such as a single peak, the town grid or a stretch of shoreline. Photos of the gondola cabins and terminals also work well, because the steep slope gives the shots a strong sense of height. Because the site is ticketed and changing, check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: On the slopes of Bob's Peak, part of Ben Lomond, directly above Queenstown and looking out over Lake Wakatipu.
text.directions_text: No station or public transport stop is listed for this spot. The map shows the position of the phone icon on the map, which is at the gondola, and the distance from where you are. Because building work is under way on the hill, follow any signs on site for the current entrance. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main view of town, lake and mountains. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the gondola cabin, the terminal buildings or the full sweep of the scene. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Walter Peak, Cecil Peak or The Remarkables.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take the wide views of the town, lake and mountains from the top viewpoint, and use the gondola or terminal as a foreground feature in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line. Keep the lake and the ridges in separate bands, and include a little foreground such as a railing or a cabin edge to show how high up you are. For the long view across the lake, try panorama mode, moving slowly and keeping the phone level. If you shoot through glass, hold the lens close to it to cut reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the distant mountains to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its detail. In low light at dusk, use night mode and brace your phone against a rail or wall to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Clear days show the most distant peaks. Late afternoon to evening usually gives softer light on the mountains, and dusk adds the town lights, but check the operating times on the official site first.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed attraction with building work going on, so check the official site before you go.
